identification: Three handmade soft red clay bricks (not 'items' of metal: the catalogue lot is '3 BROAD ARROW STAMPED CONVICT BRICKS - EX-ALANVALE NEWNHAM', i.e. bricks recovered from Alanvale, Newnham, Launceston). Each has marks hand-incised into the wet clay before firing (drawn with a finger or stick, not a stamped frog): brick 1 (larger, paler, mortar on one edge) reads roughly 'L ^ D' with a broad arrow between letters; brick 2 has a single vertical stroke beside a large broad arrow; brick 3 reads roughly 'W ^ W' (or W ^ M) with a broad arrow in the middle. Bricks 2 and 3 also show deep finger/thumb impressions at the corners, the classic sign of hand moulding seen on Tasmanian convict-made bricks. These are consistent with genuine colonial (convict-era, c.1820s-1850s) Van Diemen's Land government bricks: broad arrow plus moulder's/gang initials scratched by hand is the typical Tasmanian convict pattern; later government issue used stamped marks in a frog, not hand scratching. Provenance (Alanvale) cannot be verified from photos. Bulky-ish and heavy (3 bricks, perhaps 9-10 kg).

viewing_check: Look closely at the grooves: wet-incised marks have smooth rounded edges, slightly raised clay burr at the sides and the same fired skin inside the groove; a fresh scratch on a fired brick shows sharper edges, paler or brighter clay inside and cuts through the fire skin. Check for old lime mortar (supports building origin). Note sizes (Tasmanian convict bricks commonly about 225-240 mm). Check for chips/spalls on the marked faces.
